Some build an outline before drafting~\citep{yao2019plan,yang2022re3}, some generate a document section by section~\citep{shao2024assisting,bai2025longwriter,huot2025agents}, some recursively decompose the document into tasks~\citep{xiong2025beyond}, and some adapt plans or structural reasoning during generation~\citep{wan2025cognitive,sun2026cot}.
Across these systems, the next step is usually defined by a content unit, task node, or prescribed stage.
A complementary design question remains comparatively underexplored: should the writer decide which kind of writing process is needed next?

The cognitive process theory of writing~\citep{flower1981cognitive,hayes1996new,hayes2012modeling} provides a useful abstraction for process-level control.
\citet{flower1981cognitive} characterize writing as coordination among planning, translating, and reviewing, with a monitor deciding which process to invoke as the document develops.
This view suggests choosing the next writing process rather than the next section or task node.

Building on \citet{flower1981cognitive}, we propose \condAgenticCogWriter, a long-form writing system that implements this process-level control on top of a coding-agent-style harness with persistent state and subagent delegation (Figure~\ref{fig:agentic-cogwriter}).
A top-level Monitor agent observes the evolving draft, goals, and process history, chooses whether the next activity should be planning, drafting, or reviewing, and delegates that activity to a corresponding subagent.
The resulting process order is chosen during writing rather than fixed in advance.
We call the system \textit{agentic} for this combination: online selection of the next writing process, a persistent state shared across steps, and delegation of each selected process to a subagent.

We evaluate our system on three complementary long-form writing benchmarks spanning broad instruction-driven writing, long-context generation, and methodical expert-document production~\citep{wu2026writingbench,que2024hellobench,malaviya2025dolomites}.

In pre-specified per-benchmark pairwise tests, our system is preferred to one-shot generation in \PooledFourOneHolmCellsTotal\ of nine tests and to a fixed writing pipeline and adaptive task planning in \PooledFourTwoHolmCellsTotal\ and \PooledFourThreeHolmCellsTotal, while a post-hoc prompt-level summary across benchmarks favors it over all three.
The component analyses support a system-level interpretation: ablations that drop explicit goals or fix the process order keep most of this advantage over the alternatives.
Process traces show that \AfourCycleCompliantRate\ of complete paths conform to the planning--drafting--reviewing cycle structure and that \AfourReviewingToPlanningRate\ of runs return from reviewing to planning, so adaptive ordering is seldom used.

\paragraph{Delegation fallback.}
The prompts of our system, \condNoGoals, and \condFixedOrder\ let the \texttt{Monitor} perform a role itself when native delegation is unavailable and require it to record that fallback in the trace; the \condTaskPlanning\ prompt has no such rule.
Counting completed runs whose trace decisions mention the fallback, it occurs in \AfourFallbackRuns\ of \AfourRunCount\ runs of our system, \AfiveFallbackRuns\ of \AfiveFallbackCompleted\ of \condNoGoals, and \AsixFallbackRuns\ of \AsixFallbackCompleted\ of \condFixedOrder.

The advantage over the alternatives therefore does not rest on runs in which the \texttt{Monitor} performed a role itself.
